svg.title: Composite Index
svg.desc: Composite Index. A multi-column index serves queries that use its leading columns: put equality columns first and the range or sort column last. Step 1, Wrong column first: Only (created_at, customer_id) exists: customer 42's history walks 52,936 entries to find 20 rows. Step 2, Leftmost prefix: Swap the columns: customer_id = 42 becomes one slice of 179 entries, already sorted by created_at. Step 3, Equality first, sort last: History: seek to the slice end, read 20 entries, stop (23 buffers). Dashboard: (status, created_at). Step 4, Skip scan and the costs: Skip scan: (status, created_at) serves created_at alone too. Every index is written on every insert.

g.text: Only (created_at, customer_id) exists: customer 42's history walks 52,936 entries to find 20 rows.
Swap the columns: customer_id = 42 becomes one slice of 179 entries, already sorted by created_at.
History: seek to the slice end, read 20 entries, stop (23 buffers). Dashboard: (status, created_at).
Skip scan: (status, created_at) serves created_at alone too. Every index is written on every insert.
B-TREE LEAF ENTRIES, IN KEY ORDER
customer_id = 42 is checked on each one
already in order: no Sort node
planner would rather read the table
same query, customer with 34 orders: estimated
at 9 rows, fewer than the LIMIT, an index walk
could not stop early: it reads the table and sorts
8 kB pages touched, warm cache · PostgreSQL 18.6,
✓ one slice: seek straight to it
✓ part of the slice: seek to its start
✓ slice already sorted: read it backward
✗ no leading column: one range per customer
